sentences.text: This part reads a1, a2, a3, a4 and a6: through it, moving a1, a3 or a6 away from its first value raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99%.

Giving a2 or a4 its first value pulls it back down: with a3 = 2, a2 = 1 or a4 = 1 takes it from above 99% to below 1%, and with a6 = 2, a2 = 1 takes it from about 81% to below 1%, while with a3 = 1 or a6 = 1 it is below 1% either way.

This part adds up all six attributes with fixed weights: through it, a2 = 1 or 2 instead of 3 and a4 = 1 instead of 2 raise the predicted probability of 'yes', and moving a1, a3, a5 or a6 away from its first value or a4 from 2 to 3 lowers it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
Across the whole model, a5 = 2, 3 or 4 instead of 1 and a2 = 2 instead of 3 raise it, and a4 = 3 instead of 2 lowers it, while the typical case stays below 1%.
This gate acts on 305 of 345 training cases, 99 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on, the predicted probability of 'yes' stays below 1% with or without it.
Through it, a5 other than 1, a4 = 3 and a1 = 3 raise the probability and a3 = 2 and a6 = 2 lower it, all below 1% for the typical case it acts on.
How much a6 = 2 instead of 1 moves it depends on a5: from below 1% to above 99% when a5 is not 1, and to about 81% when a5 = 1.

This part reads only a5 and acts on 173 of 345 training cases, 65 of which are actually 'yes'; through it, a5 = 2 or 4 instead of 1 lowers the predicted probability of 'yes', though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
This unit reads a3 and is switched off: it barely changes the predictions.

lead.text: For the typical case (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1) the model gives a predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%; it adds up five parts: a sum over all six attributes, a veto on a1, a2, a3, a4 and a6, a gate on a1, a3, a4, a5 and a6, a part on a5 alone, and a unit that is switched off.

evidence.text: Through it, a2 = 1 or 2 instead of 3 and a4 = 1 instead of 2 raise the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes', and moving a1, a3, a5 or a6 away from its first value or a4 from 2 to 3 lowers it, though it stays below 1%.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

For the typical case itself, a2 = 1 or a4 = 1 lowers it through this part, and a4 = 1 counts more when a2 = 1, though it stays below 1%.

worth_checking.flag: a5 treated differently from the other attributes
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the veto reads a1, a2, a3, a4 and a6 but not a5, and another part raises the probability of 'yes' when a5 is not 1, so a5 = 1 does not count like the first value of the other attributes, as it does in the exactly-two rule.

worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the model separates values of a2 and a4 other than the first: a2 = 2 instead of 3 raises the predicted probability of 'yes' and a4 = 3 instead of 2 lowers it, which the exactly-two rule does not do.

parts.name: two_of_five_peak
parts.original_hypothesis: Two-of-five peak with an a5 handicap. The output is sigmoid(s) with s = -2.363 + Lin + Veto + 2.547*Gate - 0.599*A5 + 0.735*Inert, where Inert is identically 0. Lin (linear_first_value_score) rises by +4..+12 for each first value among a1, a2, a3, a4, a6 and is the rising edge: with at most one such first value s < 0 on all 432 configurations (max -0.42). Veto (atleast3_of_five_veto) is exactly 0 for at most two first values and <= -70 for three or more, so it is the falling edge: s < 0 for every configuration with three or more. Gate (a5_a3_bonus_gate) adds +8.5..+11 when a5 != 1 (more when a3 = 1) and nothing when a5 = 1 and a3 = 2; A5 is a -0.72 penalty for a5 in {2,4}. Net: with exactly two first values among {a1,a2,a3,a4,a6} the model predicts positive in 113 of 114 configurations when a5 != 1 but only 23 of 38 (61%) when a5 = 1 (the a5_a3 gate is weak or off there; pairs (2,3) and (3,4) always fail). So the network computes approximately 'exactly two of the five attributes a1,a2,a3,a4,a6 take their first value, and preferably a5 != 1': it agrees with [count5 == 2] on 96.3% of all 432 configurations and 95.9% of training rows, and reaches 88.7% train accuracy (AUC 0.925). Inputs a4:2, a5:2, a6:2 have no enabled connections and are zero-effect entries. Evidence: on train, ablating the veto drops accuracy 0.887 -> 0.562 and ablating the gate 0.887 -> 0.690; the score sign is negative for every configuration with <=1 or >=3 such first values. Comparison with the target rule (exactly two of all six attributes take their first value): the network has replaced a5=1 as a rule indicator with a5 != 1 as a bonus, so it is correct on two-of-six cases where a5 != 1 (113/114) but misses all 28 two-of-six cases in which a5 = 1 is one of the two, and wrongly accepts 23 of 38 three-of-six cases that include a5 = 1 (agreement with the rule 88.0% over all 432 configurations).

parts.name: atleast3_of_five_veto
parts.original_hypothesis: At-least-three-of-five veto. Node 274 = ReLU(-1.34 + 3.46 z(a1:1) + 4.56 z(a2:1) + 4.67 z(a3:1) + 3.98 z(a4:1) + 4.48 z(a6:1)) counts first-values of a1, a2, a3, a4 and a6 (a5 is NOT included). Per-indicator increments are 7.2 to 9.7 on a base of -19.2: with two or fewer indicators the pre-activation is at most -0.2 (exactly 0 output), with three it is at least +5.6. Node 2786 = ReLU(0.605*274 - 0.609) never clips while 274 is on, so the exit id_suppress = -7.14*274 - 6.56*2786 = -11.11*274 + 4.00 whenever 274 fires, i.e. a penalty of -70 or more (-269 with all five), which forces the output to 0. Exactly zero otherwise. Forms the falling edge of the response peak at three-of-five. Evidence: on all 345 training rows 274 > 0 exactly when three or more of a1,a2,a3,a4,a6 take their first value (112 rows); removing the veto drops train accuracy from 0.887 to 0.562.

parts.name: linear_first_value_score
parts.original_hypothesis: Additive per-attribute score (the linear backbone). Measured per attribute value relative to the all-low baseline, the direct edges give large positive credit when an attribute takes its first value: a6=1 +11.94, a1=1 +10.22, a2=1 +6.63, a4=1 +6.22, a3=1 +4.12, but only +2.63 for a5=1; non-first values add 0 or a penalty (a4=3 -4.60, a2=3 -3.07, a1=2 -3.00, a1=3 -1.71, a2=2 -1.91, a5=4 -0.26). Node 1948 = ReLU(0.827 - 0.090 z(a1:2)) never clips (it takes only 0.70 or 0.89), so it is an affine relay of a1:2 folded into the a1=2 penalty. The score rises roughly linearly with the number of first-values among a1, a2, a3, a4, a6 and is the rising edge of the model's response peak. Evidence: closed form is linear (sensitivities on train equal the direct weights exactly; 1948 takes only 0.70/0.89 on train, never clipping).

parts.name: a5_a3_bonus_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: A clipped bonus that rewards a5 != 1 and a3 = 1. Node 1223 = ReLU(2.47 + 1.41 z(a3:1) + 0.30 z(a4:3) - 1.86 z(a5:1) - 0.69*1717). Readout to the output (x2.547): a5 != 1 gives +12.0..13.7 when a3=1 and +4.7..6.5 when a3=2; a5 = 1 gives +1.1..2.75 when a3=1 and exactly 0 when a3=2 (clipped). So it is mostly an additive a5 != 1 bonus of ~+8.5 to +11 plus an a3=1 bonus, with one clip interaction (a5=1 and a3=2). Sub-unit 1717 = ReLU(-0.52 - 0.03 z(a1:3) - 0.05 z(a5:1) - 0.56 z(a6:1)) is near-inert: it is nonzero only when a6 != 1 and never exceeds 0.10, moving 1223 by at most 0.07. Net effect: a5 = 1 is treated as evidence AGAINST the positive class, cancelling the small direct +2.63 credit for a5=1. Evidence: on all 345 training rows 1223 = 0 exactly when a5 = 1 and a3 = 2 (40 rows); train sensitivities are dominated by a5:1 (1.65) and a3:1 (1.25), with the 1717 path < 0.15; removing the gate drops train accuracy from 0.887 to 0.690.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

units.method: raw = z * scale + mean, with the split's StandardScaler parameters (scaler_params mean and scale, fitted on the training rows)
units.round_trip_note: max |decoded - stored raw| and |re-encoded - model input| over the training rows
